title: Should Advertising to Kids Be Banned?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine advertising to children: the history from early TV hosts and Miss Francis's Ding Dong School through Mr. Potato Head's 1952 ad, kids' spending power and influence on family purchases, pester power, the scale of child-targeted ads, and research on young children's inability to recognize ads. They cover links between food marketing and childhood obesity (including the Quebec ban and priming effect), McDonald's and Happy Meal marketing, product placement, corporate ads in schools, and the American Psychology Association's position. They trace US regulation from the FCC and FTC attempts in the 1970s, Congress's pushback, Action for Children's Television, Mark Fowler's deregulation under Reagan, and the 1990 children's TV limits, then compare other countries' rules, self-regulation, online and targeted advertising, and parenting strategies like media literacy and mediation. The episode ends with listener mail about Kenner's Robin Hood toys and Rick Springfield's Star Wars collection.
topics: Robin Hood Prince of Thieves toys

segments.title: Opening banter and setup
segments.summary: Hosts plug a San Francisco Sketch Fest show, then introduce the topic of advertising to kids, recalling early TV ads and hosts pitching products.

segments.title: Early kids ads and kids' buying power
segments.summary: Early kids TV ads, including Miss Francis's Ding Dong School and Mr. Potato Head in 1952. Kids influence family purchases, with buying power estimated at $500 billion in 2000, $700 billion in 2005, and $1.2 trillion in 2012.

segments.title: Pester power and kids' allowances
segments.summary: Kids use pester power to influence parents; a survey found many parents buckle, sometimes at high cost. The hosts share childhood allowance anecdotes.

segments.title: Scale of ad spending and kids seeing ads
segments.summary: Companies spent about $17 billion on advertising aimed at kids in 2009 versus about $100 million in 1983. The 40,000 ads a year and 110 a day figures are discussed as exposure rather than viewing counts.

segments.title: Commercial Free Childhood and the case against all ads
segments.summary: Commercial Free Childhood argues kids should not see ads at all, since celebrity endorsements and characters build loyalty and undermine critical thinking.

segments.title: Children's ability to recognize ads
segments.summary: Children under four cannot distinguish commercials from programs. Recognizing persuasive intent comes around age seven, and the APA's British counterpart study concluded kids under twelve struggle. Babies reportedly link logos and mascots, and brand loyalty can form by age two.

segments.title: Food ads, childhood obesity and priming
segments.summary: Junk food ads correlate with kids eating more and rising childhood obesity. Studies show kids eat more while watching food ads and when commercials are present. Quebec's ban on fast food ads aimed at children is cited as associated with lower childhood obesity.

segments.title: Product placement, McDonald's and Happy Meal marketing
segments.summary: Product placement in TV and movies has grown. McDonald's led kid-directed fast food advertising in the 2012 Yale study, with Happy Meal ads and websites like happymeal.com and Ronald.com, plus app tie-ins with the Trolls movie.

segments.title: Advertising and commercialism in schools
segments.summary: With school budget cuts, corporations offer computer centers, vending contracts, and exclusive deals. Examples include bus advertising, a Pizza Hut reading program, and branded healthy eating kits, which imply school endorsement.

segments.title: US regulation history: FCC, FTC and Congress
segments.summary: The FCC in the 1970s proposed limits on ads to young kids, and the FTC considered a full ban. Congress stopped the FTC. Action for Children's Television took on Romper Room. Under Reagan, FCC chairman Mark Fowler pushed deregulation, and cartoon tie-ins rose sharply. The 1990 Children's Television Act set time limits and banned host selling.

segments.title: International approaches and self-regulation
segments.summary: Countries vary: the US does little, Norway and Sweden ban marketing to under-12s, and the UK and Australia have more rules plus industry self-regulation, such as not showing kids pestering parents or making kids feel inferior. Online and targeted advertising is discussed as a newer concern.

segments.title: Parenting strategies: media literacy and mediation
segments.summary: Parents can use media literacy, talking about wants and needs, co-viewing, active mediation, and restrictive mediation to reduce kids' requests. The hosts note that media literacy has fallen out of favor and that limiting screens can isolate kids. The PBS Kids Don't Buy It site is recommended.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kenner Star Wars and Robin Hood toys
segments.summary: A listener recounts Kenner repurposing its Robin Hood Prince of Thieves toys into Return of the Jedi Ewok items, and another listener reports Rick Springfield's Star Wars collection.
